cim: Megrendezték az első AI Music Awards díjátadót Los Angelesben
lead: A technikai bizonytalanságok ellenére a Sonic Intelligence Academy megrendezte a generatív zenének szentelt első nagyszabású díjátadót.
osszefoglalo:
A **Sonic Intelligence Academy** (SIQA) Los Angelesben tartotta meg az első **AI Music Awards** díjátadót, amelyet a hagyományos zeneipar mesterséges intelligenciával szembeni elutasítására válaszul hoztak létre. A szervezők célja egy olyan struktúra kiépítése, amely támogatja és elismeri az **AI-t használó alkotókat**. A nevezéshez az előadóknak regisztrálniuk kellett dalaikat a SIQA adatbázisába, megjelölve, hogy a zene teljesen AI-generált, hibrid vagy klónozott emberi hangot használ.

A rendezvényen 25 kategóriában adtak át díjakat, a főbb elismeréseket, köztük az **év előadója és az év dala** díját a Xania Monet nevű AI-persona mögött álló Telisha Jones nyerte el. A rendezvényt több szervezési és technikai fennakadás kísérte, a vendégek és alkotók személyesen vették át az elismeréseket.

A kezdeményezés a folyamatban lévő **szerzői jogi perek** és iparági viták ellenére próbál legitimációs platformot teremteni a generatív zenei műfajoknak.
miert_szamit: A zeneipari generatív AI-eszközök körüli **jogi és iparági elfogadottság** alakulása közvetlenül befolyásolja a szintetikus audio- és zenetartalmak üzleti felhasználhatóságát.

cim_eredeti: Inside the first AI Music Awards in Los Angeles, featuring AI announcers, lip-syncing, and human stand-ins, as the ceremony was mired in technical issues (Corbin Bolies/Variety)
szoveg_eredeti:
I knew things were a little off when the first thing I heard on my walk to the AI Music Awards was “the winner…” followed by the sweet voice of Kelly Clarkson.

No, Miss American Idol did not abandon her feud with the Brooklyn bird to capitalize on her newfound appreciation for AI. But as I approached the Mayan Theater in Downtown Los Angeles on a sunny afternoon to check in for Friday’s inaugural “AI Music Awards,” powered by the “Sonic Intelligence Academy” or “SIQA,” I wondered if her voice was so strong as to echo through the nearly century-old theater-turned-nightclub’s walls. To qualify for the awards, artists needed to register their tracks to SIQA’s “Verified Registry,” which denotes whether the song was fully AI-generated, made with the assistance of AI or featured a cloned human voice to lead the tune (what the group calls a “human + AI hybrid”).

Registered artists then nominate their peers in the 25 categories up for consideration — everything from “AI Song of the Year” to “Best AI Pop Song” to “Best AI Comedic Song” — and then vote on the winners. One of those nominees was Xania Monet, the AI persona of Telisha “Nikki” Jones, who a day earlier won the AI Album of the Year category at SIQA’s inaugural summit and who would eventually go on to win both artist and song of the year, three out of four of the awards’ top categories. The Sonic Intelligence Academy is the brainchild of software engineer Timirah “TJ” James and her sister Mia James. Since its January launch, it has worked to establish an awards program to counter the mainstream music industry’s aversion to AI. The group believes there needs to be infrastructure that supports those using AI to create music, rather than dismissing its existence, and it hopes to be an AI counterpart to the longstanding Recording Academy that governs the Grammy Awards. It advocates for artists to publicly associate themselves with their AI-powered work, eager to highlight the humans who helped create the product.

It’s a noble, if surprising, decision to embrace its role as counterculture when AI artists continue to pursue a Billboard charting position. Some of its methods are a little overt, perhaps intentionally: After some in the industry spurned the idea of AI-generated music charting on Billboard’s industry-standard charts, the group used a week in January ahead of the Grammys to launch its own charts exclusively for AI music. The Mayan is a 12-minute walk from the Crypto.com Arena, the Grammys’ longtime home.

The moves are not subtle, but subtlety is not the organization’s goal. The group and awards’ existence alone reflects those in the AI music space trying to move past the thorny legal questions surrounding AI music, which have led to lawsuits by artists and record labels against generators like Suno and Udio over copyright infringement, and into a realm of relevance within the genres they’re trying to em
